Sound familiar?

You don’t need a
“musical ear.”
You need a clear starting point.

Maybe the second and third tones blur together. Maybe you can say a word on its own, but lose the tone in a sentence. Or perhaps every explanation assumes you already know what to listen for.

Mandarin tones are learnable patterns of relative pitch. You don’t need to hit a particular musical note. You need to understand the movement—and practice it in your own comfortable voice.

Start with the shape of each tone. Then learn what happens when tones meet.

Your first small breakthrough

The four Mandarin tones,
made visible.

In Mandarin Chinese, the same syllable can mean different things depending on its tone. Here’s a simple introduction using ma.

01 / FIRST TONEā

High & level

Keep your pitch steady at a comfortable high level.

māmother
02 / SECOND TONEá

Rising

Start around the middle of your range, then move upward.

máhemp
03 / THIRD TONEǎ

Low & dipping

Dip low. In isolation, the full tone rises again at the end.

mǎhorse
04 / FOURTH TONEà

Falling

Begin high and drop decisively. Keep your voice relaxed.

màto scold
And the neutral tone?

It’s short and light, with no tone mark. Its pitch depends on the preceding tone—like ma, the question particle.

Try this first

Trace it. Say it. Notice the movement.

Move your finger along each curve while slowly saying the syllable. Keep your volume comfortable; change the pitch, not the loudness. This visual warm-up is a starting point. Compare your pronunciation with a reliable native-speaker model as you practice.

The next step is putting tones together.

In everyday speech, the third tone often stays low, and neighboring tones can change how a word sounds. The ebook walks you through these details.

A few things you might be wondering

Before you begin.

Clear answers, so you can decide whether this guide fits your next step.

Is this ebook suitable for beginners?

Yes. It starts with why Mandarin tones matter and introduces the four main tones and neutral tone before moving into practice, tone pairs and tone changes. It is also useful for learners revisiting the basics.

Do I need perfect pitch to learn Mandarin tones?

No. Mandarin tones use relative pitch: the movement of your voice within your own range. The guide helps you understand those movements and practice them deliberately.

What’s the difference between the second and third tones?

The second tone rises from a middle pitch. The third tone is centered on a low pitch; its full, isolated form dips and rises, but in connected speech it often stays low. The ebook explores those differences and common errors.

Does it cover tone sandhi?

Yes. It includes third-tone sandhi, sequences of third tones, and tone-change rules for bù and yī, along with other minor tone changes.

What format is the ebook?

It is a 61-page PDF written in English, with written explanations, visual guidance, examples and exercises. The product offered here is an ebook; no separate audio course is advertised.

How do I buy it, and what does it cost?

Choose “Get the ebook” to continue to Hotmart. The current price, available payment methods, purchase terms and delivery information are shown there before you complete your order.

Will this make me fluent in Mandarin?

This guide focuses on tones and pronunciation. Fluency also involves vocabulary, grammar, listening and conversation. Progress depends on consistent practice and feedback; the ebook does not promise fluency within a set time.
